exit_trigger: Evidence that customers can switch suppliers without performance risk, eroding pricing power; Sustained decline in ROE well below 15% without a one-off explanation; Debt-to-equity moving materially above 0.5 to fund acquisitions or buybacks at high prices; Management dishonesty or serious capital allocation failures; Price persistently above 1.5x a conservatively computed intrinsic value
rationale: I own this one, and I'm down 21.31% on it since August, which tells me about the price and nothing yet about the business. What I can verify says it is a good business. Five-year average ROE is 30.6%, debt-to-equity is 0.497 (right at my 0.5 line, with no room to spare), and five-year average owner earnings are about $413 million against a $6.56 billion market cap. The model's 45% margin of safety leans on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, which is more generous than I like, so I discount that number. Still, a price drop with no evidence that the moat has weakened is no reason to sell. I'll keep what I own and add only if the missing evidence, a ten-year earnings record and management's capital allocation, confirms the quality.

exit_trigger: Evidence that the brand can no longer raise prices without losing volume; Sustained decline in ROE or owner earnings that signals a weakening moat; Management destroying value through poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Disclosure problems or dishonesty by management; Price exceeding 1.5x a conservatively re-derived intrinsic value, persistently
rationale: I own these shares, bought at $128.38 and now marked at $109.71, down 14.54% after 95 days. A price decline alone is no reason to sell, so the question is whether the brand is still doing its job. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 34.6%, a reported debt-to-equity of 0.0, and 5-year average owner earnings of about $1.32 billion against a $12.1 billion market cap. That is the economics of a real franchise. But the model's $346.97 intrinsic value rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I distrust a number that flattering, so I take the headline 68% margin of safety with a large grain of salt. Athletic apparel sits close to the fashion line I have avoided for decades, and the snapshot gives me no 10-year earnings record, no CEO tenure and no pricing-power evidence. I will hold the position and not add until I can verify those, and I will sell if the brand's pricing power visibly erodes.

exit_trigger: Evidence that franchise relationships or service profitability are eroding materially; Management destroys value through large acquisitions at peak prices; Price exceeds 1.5x intrinsic value persistently; Sustained deterioration in ROE below 15% or debt-to-equity above 0.5
rationale: I own six shares of Penske Automotive Group, bought at $216.77 and now at $213.10, so I'm down about 1.7% after 95 days. That is noise, not information. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.39, and a price about 18% below my owner-earnings value of $259.62, which clears my 15% threshold. But I have to be honest about the limits here: the snapshot says nothing about earnings consistency over ten years, ROIC, or management, and the valuation assumes zero growth at a 5% discount rate, so I can't confirm every criterion. A car dealer's moat is thin and rests on service, scale and a premium and commercial-truck mix, and I'd not add until I could verify those. I keep what I own, I don't add on this evidence, and I'll let the business show me more.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power or customer switching away from its supply programs; Sustained decline in ROE below 15% without a clear temporary cause; Management capital-allocation failures such as value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; A materially better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: I own this one, and fifteen days in the shares are down about half a percent from my entry at $120.05, which tells me nothing about the business. The numbers I can see are decent: market cap of about $6.7 billion, five-year average ROE of 20.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, and a computed margin of safety of 24% against an intrinsic value of $157.18. But I have to be honest about the weak spots. That value leans on 8% growth, a trailing 9% CAGR capped at 8%, and owner earnings of $303 million are only about 4.5% of the market cap, so the discount is not as generous as it looks. The ten-year earnings record, CEO tenure and insider activity are not in what I was given, so I cannot call those criteria met. I keep the position at its current size, add nothing until I can verify those gaps, and sell only if the moat erodes, not because the price wiggles.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand or channel erosion, such as sustained loss of share to lower-cost rivals or private-label products; Technology shift (for example away from tank water heaters) that the company fails to lead or adapt to; Management destroying value through a large overpriced acquisition or a break in candor with shareholders; Price rising above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Sustained fall of ROE well below 15% without a clear temporary cause
rationale: We own this one, and I'm content to keep sitting on it. It makes water heaters and water treatment products, a business I can explain in two paragraphs, and the snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 23.7% with debt-to-equity of only 0.08. That is the kind of capital-light, low-debt compounding I like. My owner-earnings estimate puts value near $95.72 a share against a price of $63.88, a 33% margin of safety, though that rests on 8% growth capped from a trailing 8.8% and a 5% discount rate, so I hold it loosely. We've owned it only 18 days and are up 3.9%, which tells me nothing about the business. I haven't verified ten years of earnings history or management tenure from this snapshot, so I'm holding rather than adding until those checks are done.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained inability to pass through cost increases; Sustained fall in ROE well below 15% without a one-off explanation; Debt verification reveals leverage far above the reported 0.003 debt-to-equity; Management making large value-destroying acquisitions or showing dishonest reporting; Price rising above 1.5x intrinsic value on a persistent basis
rationale: We own 12 shares, bought 12 days ago at $103.57 and now up 3.21%, so the question is whether to keep them, and I would. This is a coatings and sealants business I can describe in two paragraphs, and the snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 22.9% and 5-year average owner earnings of about $593 million. At $106.89 against my $133.59 estimate, the margin of safety is about 20%, above my 15% bar, though the estimate leans on 8% growth that is capped from a 9.5% trailing rate. Two things keep me from adding: the reported debt-to-equity of 0.003 looks too low to take on faith until I confirm the debt is fully captured, and the snapshot gives no 10-year earnings record, CEO tenure or insider data. We hold, we don't chase, and we let time work.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power or declining installed-base retention; Management making value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Technological disruption that undermines the switching-cost advantage in process automation; Price above 1.5 times a conservatively recomputed intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: I don't own Emerson today, and the question is whether to start. The numbers I can see are attractive: a 30.6% five-year average ROE with debt-to-equity of 0.44, and a model margin of safety of 38.7% against a price of $167.71. But that intrinsic value of $273.41 rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, which works out to about 29 times five-year average owner earnings. I'd want to haircut that before relying on it. The snapshot does not give me ten years of earnings history, CEO tenure, ROIC, or the Treasury yield for my earnings-yield check. I won't buy on the handful of fields that happen to look good. I'll keep Emerson on the watch list and wait for those gaps to be filled or for a price that clears even a conservative valuation.

exit_trigger: Evidence that the cost advantage is eroding, such as sustained margin compression versus peers or loss of share to lower-cost imports; Substitution of copper tube and fittings by alternative materials at scale in core end markets; Management destroying value through large acquisitions at peak prices or dishonest reporting; Price exceeding 1.5x a conservatively re-based intrinsic value with the gap persisting; Verification showing that earnings are too cyclical or inconsistent to pass the ten-year earnings test
rationale: We own this one, and it is a few days old, so I won't pretend the position has proven anything yet. It is a simple business: it turns copper and other metals into tube, fittings and related products, and its scale is the edge. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 29.3% and a debt-to-equity of 0.0, and the owner earnings figure is solid. But the 67% margin of safety comes from a model that assumes 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on that for a metal-linked business. I'm keeping the shares and not adding until I can verify the ten-year earnings record, management's capital allocation and how durable the cost edge is. This isn't a moat like Coca-Cola's, and I'll hold only as long as the cost advantage stays intact.
